Tariffs Defied, a Court Report Sealed, and a Congressman Removed Twice

A Supreme Court loss becomes a same-day workaround, Epstein files reveal new gaps, and a State of the Union turns into a stage for protest and arrest

```markdown This week began with a defeat for the presidency and ended, in practice, as something closer to a demonstration of how little a defeat can mean. On Saturday, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that President Trump's global tariffs, imposed under emergency economic powers, were unconstitutional — a reminder that the power to tax and regulate commerce belongs to Congress, not the executive alone. Within a day, the White House announced a new 10 percent global tariff under a different statute, then raised it to 15 percent. Confusion followed almost immediately: businesses were unsure whether refunds were owed, European trade officials paused a pending ratification, and legal analysts debated whether the new tariffs were simply the old ones wearing a different label. It was the first and clearest expression of a pattern that would recur throughout the week — adverse rulings treated not as boundaries but as prompts to find another route to the same destination.

The weekend also brought a string of courtroom setbacks for federal immigration enforcement. Judges in Minneapolis and Los Angeles dismissed assault charges against men accused of confronting ICE officers, in both cases because sworn statements from federal agents conflicted with video evidence or were internally inconsistent. These were not isolated technical dismissals; they raised pointed questions about the reliability of the government's own account of enforcement encounters. Meanwhile, a government funding standoff forced TSA to suspend PreCheck and Global Entry over staffing shortages — PreCheck was restored within twelve hours after industry pressure, but Global Entry remained down, a small but telling sign of how quickly a funding fight can degrade everyday public services. Elsewhere over the weekend, the Justice Department intervened to back a lawsuit challenging Los Angeles school district equity policies as discriminatory against white students, a federal appeals court allowed Louisiana's mandatory Ten Commandments classroom law to take effect, and ICE detained a longtime Michigan resident with a pending deportation appeal along with a British tourist holding a valid visa for six weeks — cases that, together with continuing protests in North Carolina against a planned detention center expansion, showed enforcement pressing against even settled legal residents and visitors.

By Monday, three threads had emerged that would run through the rest of the week. The Department of Justice's release of files related to Jeffrey Epstein continued to ripple through academic and media institutions, prompting resignations, faculty reviews, and cancellations at Columbia, Harvard, Yale, and CBS as previously hidden connections came to light. Separately, Judge Aileen Cannon — a Trump appointee — permanently blocked the release of the second volume of Special Counsel Jack Smith's report on the handling of classified documents, with the Justice Department declining to contest the motion. That decision effectively sealed a significant investigative record on a former president's conduct from both Congress and the public, permanently. And a former ICE training instructor, Ryan Schwank, testified to Congress that officer training hours had been cut and that instruction had included guidance on entering homes without warrants — testimony serious enough that he resigned in protest after giving it. A Texas judge, meanwhile, ordered the release of a five-year-old asylum seeker who had been detained with his father, criticizing the government's justification for holding a child. On the tariff front, FedEx sued for refunds and Illinois Governor JB Pritzker sent the White House a symbolic $8.7 billion invoice for tariff-related costs to state families — early signs that industry and state governments intended to keep pressing the legal question the Court had just settled. House Republicans also passed a resolution using the Congressional Review Act to overturn a mining moratorium near Minnesota's Boundary Waters, part of a broader effort to apply the expedited tool retroactively to environmental protections.

Tuesday's State of the Union address turned into the week's most visible flashpoint. Aliya Rahman, a disabled guest of Rep. Ilhan Omar, was forcibly arrested by Capitol Police for standing silently in the gallery. Rep. Al Green was separately removed for holding up a sign protesting a racially charged video the president had shared about the Obamas. Both incidents put security power on public display, aimed not at any disruption but at symbolic and silent dissent inside the chamber itself. At least 40 Democratic members of Congress skipped the speech entirely, opting instead for a "People's State of the Union" event on the National Mall organized by outside groups — a boycott large enough to represent real institutional estrangement from a presidential ritual rather than a scattered protest. In his remarks, Trump claimed the Supreme Court's tariff ruling had actually given him "far more powers" and threatened higher tariffs on countries that "play games," even as House Speaker Mike Johnson acknowledged, separately, that Congress had no appetite to formally codify the tariffs Trump was already imposing — a gap between claimed authority and actual legislative backing that went largely unresolved. The same day, Senate Democrats opened an investigation into whether FCC Chair Brendan Carr and Paramount had blocked a Stephen Colbert interview to benefit the administration amid a pending merger review.

Wednesday deepened the Epstein-files story considerably. NPR and the New York Times reported that the Justice Department had withheld more than 50 pages of FBI interviews with a woman accusing Trump of sexual abuse as a minor — a disclosure gap that appeared to conflict directly with the Epstein Files Transparency Act Congress had passed. House Democrats opened a formal probe. It was the clearest evidence yet that transparency commitments around the Epstein files might bend when they touched the president himself, and it connected directly back to the sealed Jack Smith report from two days earlier — two separate legal mechanisms, in the same week, both working to keep records concerning the president's conduct out of public view. There was a countervailing note: a magistrate judge blocked the Justice Department from searching the electronic devices of Washington Post reporter Hannah Natanson, criticizing the government's legal filing and citing First Amendment concerns — a rare, clean press-freedom win. The Justice Department also sued UCLA over alleged campus antisemitism tied to pro-Palestinian protests, part of a widening legal campaign against universities in Democratic-led states. And Vice President Vance announced that the administration would withhold $259.5 million in Medicaid reimbursements from Minnesota over fraud concerns; state officials called the move politically motivated, and later reporting connected it to sentiment surrounding the state's Somali population — the clearest instance yet of federal spending power being wielded against a specific, disfavored state population rather than applied neutrally.

Thursday brought a case that fused several of the week's concerns into one episode. DHS agents, posing falsely as police searching for a missing child, arrested Columbia student Elmina Aghayeva; she was released only after direct intervention from both President Trump and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, drawing criticism for the use of deception as an enforcement tactic. In Kansas, lawmakers overrode the governor's veto to enact a law invalidating transgender residents' driver's licenses and permitting private lawsuits against transgender people in restrooms, stripping legal recognition from an entire class of state residents in one legislative stroke. DHS separately awarded a $250,000 public-relations contract to a Republican consulting firm with ties to former Trump campaign officials, following a 31-hour bidding window that reportedly required demonstrated loyalty to administration policy — a striking departure from standard procurement neutrality. An Oregon federal judge, meanwhile, ruled against the administration's abandonment of a Biden-era agreement protecting endangered Columbia and Snake River salmon, finding the government had presented evidence contradicting the established scientific record. And the EPA repealed the endangerment finding that underlies federal greenhouse gas regulation, while rolling back offshore wind approvals and clean energy incentives — a move tied to an estimated 170,000 clean energy jobs lost or delayed, and one that dismantled a foundational legal basis for climate policy built up over more than a decade.

Friday extended several of these threads to their sharpest points. The EPA followed its repeal of the endangerment finding with blanket exemptions for 71 coal plants from mercury and air toxics rules dating to 2024, in some cases granting longer exemptions than requested even where compliance technology already existed. Federal authorities arrested 25 more people connected to a January anti-ICE protest at a St. Paul church, bringing the total charged to 39 — a scale of prosecution over a single demonstration that signaled a widening use of criminal charges against organized dissent. A nearly blind Rohingya refugee, released from federal custody and driven miles from his home without notice to his family or attorney, was later found dead; the agency described the drop-off as a courtesy, a characterization that sat uneasily against his evident vulnerability. Elsewhere, a federal judge blocked DHS from detaining lawfully admitted refugees solely for not yet adjusting to permanent resident status, reaffirming statutory limits on detention authority, and raids at California fast food locations triggered fear and walkouts among workers, prompting a local union to draft a pledge urging employers to require judicial warrants before granting ICE access to workplaces. Community pressure in Concord, North Carolina led property owners to publicly reject leasing space for a planned ICE facility, even as a state elections board advanced new voting restrictions based on unsubstantiated noncitizen-voting claims. Perhaps most consequentially, right-wing activists circulated a draft executive order that would declare a national emergency over debunked 2020 election-interference claims in order to assert federal control over voting processes, including bans on mail-in ballots and voting machines — a proposal legal experts described as unconstitutional on its face. A separate Republican legal filing sought to revive the independent state legislature theory, aiming to insulate gerrymandered maps from state court review.

Taken as a whole, the week displayed a government whose formal checks were functioning — courts dismissed weak prosecutions, blocked improper detentions, protected a journalist's sources, and struck down an unlawful tariff regime — while the executive branch and allied state legislatures worked, often successfully, to route around each of those checks rather than absorb them. A Supreme Court ruling became a same-day workaround. A congressional transparency law met a records gap. A disabled bystander's silence in a public gallery met physical removal. A state's Medicaid funding met a freeze tied to who its residents were. None of this required the machinery of government to break; it required only that adverse rulings be treated as starting points for negotiation rather than as settled boundaries — a distinction that, multiplied across a single week, says a great deal about where authority in American governance was actually being tested. ```
